articles.label: Analysis
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on consultants than actual drainage projects. Flooding season is here.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.2 million from the stormwater fee since 2023 but completed only 12 of 89 promised drainage projects
Public records show $8.3 million spent on engineering consultants and administrative costs while residents in flood-prone areas wait for relief
County commissioners approved another $2.1 million consulting contract in June despite growing backlog of shovel-ready projects
articles.body:
The water rose fast on Doris Avenue last September. Four inches of rain in two hours turned the Brownsville neighborhood street into a canal. Teresa Macklin watched from her porch as the drainage ditch behind her house overflowed and sent muddy water across her backyard, through her garage, and into her living room for the third time in eighteen months.

"They told us when we voted for that fee that this would get fixed," Macklin said. "That was three years ago. Nothing's changed except I pay more on my water bill."

Macklin pays $7.50 a month. So does every other residential property owner in unincorporated Escambia County. Commercial properties pay more based on impervious surface area. Since the stormwater utility fee took effect in October 2023, the county has collected $47.2 million dedicated exclusively to drainage improvements.

The money is sitting in a designated fund. The projects are not getting built.

The Numbers Don't Add Up

When commissioners approved the fee structure in 2022, county staff presented voters with a list of 89 priority drainage projects. The estimated cost: $156 million over ten years. The fee would generate roughly $16 million annually, enough to tackle the worst flooding areas within the first five years.

Three years in, the county has completed twelve projects. Total construction cost: $11.4 million.

Administrative and consulting expenses tell a different story. According to financial records obtained through a public records request, the county has spent $8.3 million on engineering consultants, project managers and program administration since the fee launched. That's 73 cents spent on overhead for every dollar spent actually moving dirt.

"These projects require extensive engineering and permitting," said County Administrator Wes Moreno at a June 13 commission meeting. "You can't just show up with a backhoe."

Moreno is not wrong about the complexity. Stormwater projects require hydraulic modeling, environmental permits, easement acquisition and coordination with state agencies. What he did not explain is why the county awarded another $2.1 million consulting contract in June to a firm that has already received $3.4 million since 2023.

The firm, Coastal Engineering Partners of Mobile, was hired to provide "program management services" for the stormwater utility. Their scope includes overseeing other consultants who do the actual engineering design.

A Backlog Growing Faster Than Progress

The original 89-project list has grown to 127. Flooding complaints filed with the county's stormwater division increased 34% between 2024 and 2025. Staff attributed the spike to heavier rainfall and aging infrastructure, but residents in affected neighborhoods have a simpler explanation: word got out that the county was collecting money for drainage work.

"People figured if they complained loud enough, they'd get on the list," said Marcus Webb, who lives on Fairfield Drive near the intersection that floods during routine afternoon thunderstorms. "Now everybody's on the list and nobody's getting fixed."

Webb's intersection sits at project number 47 on the current priority ranking. At the current pace of completion—four projects per year—he would wait until 2038.

The prioritization methodology itself has drawn criticism. Projects are scored on factors including flooding frequency, property damage potential and environmental impact. But the formula also includes "project readiness," which rewards projects that already have engineering complete. Since the consultants determine which projects get engineered first, they effectively control the priority list.

"It's a self-licking ice cream cone," said District 4 Commissioner Robert Cole at the June meeting. Cole voted against the latest consulting contract. He was the only one.

Where the Money Goes

The stormwater utility fund operates separately from the county's general budget. State law requires the fees be spent only on stormwater purposes. But "stormwater purposes" is a broad category.

Beyond the $8.3 million in consulting and administrative costs, the fund has paid for:

  • $2.1 million for new vehicles and equipment for the stormwater division
  • $1.8 million for ditch maintenance countywide
  • $890,000 for a public education campaign about stormwater pollution
  • $340,000 for software to track complaints and projects

All of these expenses are legal. Whether they represent the best use of a fee sold to voters as a fix for neighborhood flooding is a separate question.

"People voted to stop their houses from flooding," said Macklin, the Brownsville resident. "I don't remember anything on the ballot about buying trucks or making commercials."

The public education campaign, which launched in early 2025, includes television ads, social media content and school programs about keeping pollutants out of storm drains. The contractor, a Pensacola marketing firm, received a three-year deal worth $1.2 million.

Commissioners Defend the Pace

District 2 Commissioner Steven Barry, whose district includes some of the worst flooding areas, said the criticism reflects unrealistic expectations about government infrastructure projects.

"Rome wasn't built in a day," Barry said in an interview. "We have to do this right. If we rush and a project fails, we've wasted money and made the problem worse."

Barry pointed to the completed projects as evidence of progress. The Navy Boulevard drainage improvements cost $3.2 million and reduced flooding in a commercial corridor. The West Pensacola retention pond project, at $1.9 million, captures runoff that previously flowed into Bayou Chico.

"Those are real improvements that help real people," Barry said. "More are coming."

The county's five-year capital plan shows 23 stormwater projects scheduled for construction through 2028. If all are completed on budget, they would represent roughly $38 million in drainage improvements. That would still leave the program behind pace to complete the original project list within the promised timeframe, and the list keeps growing.

Hurricane Season Complicates Everything

June 1 marked the start of Atlantic hurricane season. Forecasters predict above-average activity through November. The last major hurricane to hit Escambia County directly was Sally in 2020, which dropped more than 20 inches of rain on some areas and caused catastrophic flooding.

A storm of similar intensity would overwhelm the county's drainage infrastructure regardless of how many projects get completed in the next few months. But for residents in flood-prone neighborhoods, every rainy season without improvement feels like borrowed time.

"I put everything valuable up on blocks now," said Webb. "That's my flood control program."

The county maintains an emergency operations fund separate from the stormwater utility, and FEMA assistance would be available for a declared disaster. But the stormwater fee was supposed to address the routine flooding that happens without any hurricane involvement—the afternoon thunderstorms that turn streets into rivers, the drainage ditches that overflow after an inch of rain.

Macklin said she has considered selling her house and moving somewhere with better drainage. The problem is disclosure.

"I'd have to tell buyers it floods," she said. "Who's going to pay full price for that?"

What Happens Next

The Board of County Commissioners will review the stormwater utility's performance at a workshop scheduled for August 8. Staff have been directed to prepare a comprehensive report on project status, spending and timeline projections.

Commissioner Cole said he intends to propose a cap on administrative spending as a percentage of annual revenue. His proposal would limit overhead to 15% and require the remaining 85% be spent on construction.

"The voters approved this fee for one reason," Cole said. "We need to deliver or we need to explain why we can't."

Whether his colleagues support the restriction remains unclear. The consulting contracts that have consumed much of the program's budget were approved with 4-1 votes, Cole dissenting each time.

Meanwhile, the fund balance continues to grow. As of June 30, the stormwater utility held $27.3 million in reserves—money collected but not yet spent on anything. At current collection rates, that figure will exceed $40 million by the end of 2027.

Teresa Macklin will be watching the sky this summer, same as every summer. The drainage ditch behind her house looks the same as it did when she voted for the stormwater fee in 2022. The water bill is higher. Everything else is waiting.

articles.label: Housing
articles.headline: The Last Mobile Home Parks on Pensacola Beach Are Running Out of Time
articles.dek: Rising land values and expiring leases threaten to displace dozens of year-round residents from the island. Most have nowhere else to go.
brief: Two mobile home parks on Pensacola Beach house roughly 80 year-round residents, many of them service workers and retirees who have lived on the island for decades.
Lease agreements with the Santa Rosa Island Authority expire in 2028 and 2031, and rising land values make renewal at current rates increasingly unlikely.
Residents say they cannot afford to relocate to the mainland, where rents have doubled since 2020, and no affordable housing exists on the barrier island.
articles.body:
The wind off Santa Rosa Sound smells like salt and outboard motor oil. At Paradise Mobile Home Park, a quarter mile from the public beach access on Via de Luna, Linda Faye Hutchins waters a pot of lantana on her wooden deck. She has lived in lot 17 for nineteen years.

"I know what's coming," she said. "I just don't know when."

Hutchins, 71, retired from housekeeping at the Holiday Inn Express in 2022. Her monthly lot rent is $485. Her mobile home, a 1998 Fleetwood with hurricane straps bolted to concrete footings, is worth maybe $8,000. The land beneath it is worth considerably more.

Paradise is one of two mobile home parks remaining on Pensacola Beach. Together they house roughly 80 year-round residents on Santa Rosa Island Authority land. The leases that allow them to exist expire in 2028 and 2031. What happens after that is unclear. What seems certain is that mobile homes will not be part of the answer.

An Accidental Community

The parks date to the 1960s, when Pensacola Beach was still a quiet fishing destination and the island authority leased land cheaply to encourage development. Mobile homes made sense. They were affordable, hurricane-removable, and attracted the workers who staffed the motels and bait shops.

That economy is gone. The motels became condominiums. The bait shops became oyster bars. Land that leased for $50 a year in 1965 now commands rates that bear no relationship to what a retired housekeeper can pay.

"The island has changed around us," said Marcus Delacroix, 58, who drives a shuttle van for Pensacola Beach RV Resort and has lived at Tropical Breeze Mobile Home Park since 2009. "We didn't change. We're still here doing the same jobs. But now we're in the way."

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, a state-created body that manages development on the beach, has not announced plans for either property. Board chair Patricia Salazar declined to comment on lease negotiations, citing ongoing discussions with park owners.

"The authority has to balance multiple interests," Salazar said at the board's June meeting. "We're aware of the residents' concerns."

The Math Doesn't Work

According to Escambia County property records, the Paradise Mobile Home Park parcel is assessed at $2.1 million. The Tropical Breeze parcel, slightly larger, is assessed at $2.4 million. Both sit within walking distance of the beach and the island's commercial core.

Comparable leaseholds on Pensacola Beach—the island operates on a leasehold system rather than fee-simple ownership—generate annual rents of $15,000 to $40,000 per unit for condominium developments. The mobile home parks generate a fraction of that.

"From a pure revenue standpoint, those parcels are underperforming," said Raymond Oster, a commercial real estate broker with Levin Rinke who specializes in beach properties. "The authority has a fiduciary responsibility to the island. At some point, that math becomes hard to ignore."

For residents, the math is simpler and more brutal. The median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in Pensacola proper has risen to $1,340 per month, according to Zillow data from June 2026. That's up from $675 in January 2020.

Hutchins receives $1,847 per month from Social Security. Her lot rent, utilities and insurance consume roughly half of that. A mainland apartment would consume nearly all of it.

"Where am I supposed to go?" she said. "I've looked. There's nothing I can afford. Nothing."

The Invisible Workforce

Pensacola Beach markets itself as a laid-back alternative to Panama City and Destin—less crowded, more authentic, the kind of place where bartenders remember your name. That authenticity depends in part on workers who actually live on the island rather than commuting from the mainland.

A 2024 study commissioned by the Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce found that 62 percent of island service workers commuted from Pensacola or Gulf Breeze. Of those who lived on the beach, nearly half resided in the two mobile home parks.

"You take away those parks, you take away your most experienced employees," said Donna Kirby, general manager of Flounder's Chowder House, one of the island's largest restaurants. "These are people who work doubles during spring break, who show up during hurricanes to board windows. You can't replace that with someone driving over the bridge."

Kirby said she has already lost three longtime employees to rising rents on the mainland. She does not know how she would replace the seven current employees who live in the mobile home parks.

The island has no workforce housing program. A 2019 proposal to allow accessory dwelling units on residential leaseholds was rejected by the island authority board after opposition from neighboring homeowners.

Running Out the Clock

At Tropical Breeze, the lease expires in December 2031. Park owner Gerald Tatum, 73, said he has received inquiries from three separate developers interested in the property. He has not responded to any of them.

"I'm 73 years old," Tatum said, sitting in a plastic chair outside the park's laundry building. "I've owned this place for 31 years. I know every person here. You think I want to be the one who throws them out?"

Tatum said he hopes to negotiate a lease extension that would allow the park to continue operating through 2040. He acknowledged that the authority has made no commitment to such an extension.

"I'm trying to buy time," he said. "That's all I can do. Buy time and hope something changes."

At Paradise, the timeline is shorter. The lease expires in March 2028—less than two years away. Park manager Sheila Robichaux said she has received no formal communication from the authority about whether the lease will be renewed.

"We're in limbo," Robichaux said. "The residents ask me what's going to happen and I can't tell them anything because nobody's told me anything."

No Good Options

Florida law provides some protections for mobile home park residents facing closure. Under the Florida Mobile Home Act, park owners must give residents at least six months' notice before closing a park and must provide relocation assistance of at least $3,000 per household.

For most Paradise and Tropical Breeze residents, $3,000 would not cover first and last month's rent on a mainland apartment, let alone the cost of moving a mobile home—which typically runs $5,000 to $15,000 depending on distance and setup requirements.

And moving is only possible if a mobile home is new enough to be accepted elsewhere. Most parks will not accept units older than 15 years. The average age of mobile homes at Paradise and Tropical Breeze exceeds 20 years.

"My home is worthless anywhere but here," said Delacroix. "I can't move it. I can't sell it. If they close this park, I lose everything."

Some residents have begun making contingency plans. Three households at Tropical Breeze have purchased small RVs, hoping to find space at campgrounds if the park closes. Two residents at Paradise have moved in with family members on the mainland, keeping their mobile homes as weekend retreats while they still can.

Hutchins has no family in the area. Her daughter lives in Oregon. Her son died in 2018.

"This is my home," she said. "This is where I want to die. I know that sounds dramatic. But at my age, you think about these things."

She turned off the hose and sat down in a folding chair facing the sound. A pelican dove into the water fifty yards out and came up with something silver in its beak.

"I've got two years," she said. "Maybe less. I try not to think about it too much."

The lantana in the pot beside her was blooming orange and yellow. She planted it in 2019. It comes back every year.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's Gate Traffic Is About to Get Worse
articles.dek: A summer construction project will close the Navy Boulevard entrance for six weeks starting Monday. Here's what commuters need to know.
brief: The Navy Boulevard gate at NAS Pensacola will close for six weeks starting Monday, July 20, for infrastructure upgrades to the entry control point.
All traffic will be redirected to the Blue Angel Parkway gate, with base officials warning of delays of 30 minutes or more during peak hours.
The closure affects roughly 8,000 daily commuters who use the Navy Boulevard entrance, including civilian employees and contractors.
articles.body:
The line at NAS Pensacola's Blue Angel Parkway gate already stretches past the Waffle House most mornings. Starting Monday, it's going to get longer.

Naval Air Station Pensacola announced Friday that the Navy Boulevard gate will close for six weeks beginning July 20 to allow for infrastructure upgrades at the entry control point. The project includes new vehicle barriers, upgraded security screening equipment and repaving of the inspection lanes.

"We understand this will create inconvenience for our workforce and visitors," said Lt. Cmdr. Sarah Chen, public affairs officer for NAS Pensacola. "We've timed this project to coincide with reduced summer training schedules, but there's no way to do this work without some disruption."

The Navy Boulevard entrance handles approximately 8,000 vehicles per day during normal operations, according to base figures. That traffic will now funnel through the Blue Angel Parkway gate on the station's west side.

What to Expect

Base officials are warning commuters to expect delays of 30 minutes or more during peak entry times, typically 6:30 to 8 a.m. and 3:30 to 5 p.m. The base is recommending personnel adjust their schedules where possible.

"If you can come in at 6 instead of 7, do it," Chen said. "If your command allows flexible arrival times, take advantage of that."

The closure affects civilian employees, contractors, military personnel and anyone with business on the installation. The National Naval Aviation Museum, which draws tourists through the west entrance, should see minimal impact since most visitors already use Blue Angel Parkway.

Delivery vehicles and commercial traffic will be routed to a temporary inspection point near the museum entrance. Large trucks should expect additional screening time.

The Construction

The Navy Boulevard entry control point was last upgraded in 2014. The current project will install Delta Scientific vehicle barriers capable of stopping a 15,000-pound truck at 50 miles per hour—the current Department of Defense standard for high-traffic military installations.

The work also includes new license plate readers, upgraded credential scanners and a reconfigured inspection lane that base officials say will eventually reduce wait times once the project is complete.

Turner Construction is the prime contractor. The $4.2 million project is funded through the Navy's annual facilities maintenance budget.

Alternate Routes

Commuters approaching from downtown Pensacola or the east side will feel the closure most acutely. Base officials suggest taking I-110 south to I-10 west, then exiting at Blue Angel Parkway—a route that adds roughly four miles but avoids surface street congestion on Navy Boulevard.

Those coming from the north can take Mobile Highway to Blue Angel Parkway. Commuters from Gulf Breeze and Pensacola Beach will see little change to their normal routes.

The base is coordinating with Escambia County traffic management to adjust signal timing on Blue Angel Parkway during the construction period.

The Navy Boulevard gate is scheduled to reopen August 31. Chen said the base will provide weekly updates on the project's progress through its official Facebook page and the NAS Pensacola website.
